newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf ministers to meet in Riyadh on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Gulf ministers to meet in Riyadh on Sunday.

text.p: Foreign and finance ministers from the six Gulf Arab states will meet in Riyadh on Sunday for talks on regional development and the long-awaited unification of their customs tariffs.

The Riyadh-based Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) said in a statement on Thursday that the ministers of finance, in separate talks, would focus on steps taken so far to unify customs to open the door for free trade with other economic blocs.
Differences have been blocking such an agreement almost since the alliance's formation 15 years ago and a political decision is needed, Arab diplomats say.

GCC and European Union foreign ministers agreed in talks in April to set a deadline of no more than two years to complete free trade accord between the two trading partners -- an issue under discussion for more than a decade.
Unifying GCC standard tariffs, which vary from four to 12 percent, is among key EU demands for a free trade accord which could open lucrative European markets to cheap petrochemicals from the Gulf.

Arab diplomats said the foreign ministers would also discuss GCC ties with Iran and Iraq, the Arab-Israeli conflict and the outcome of Saudi and GCC efforts to convince the emir of Bahrain to attend the next Gulf Arab summit in Qatar.

The Riyadh meeting comes amid a flurry of contacts by Gulf Arab officials to prepare for the December 7 summit of heads of state of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan and Minister of State Abdul-Aziz bin Abdullah al-Khoweiter returned home on Wednesday after brief separate visits to Manama and Doha.
Bahrain has threatened to boycott the next summit because of a territorial dispute with Qatar.
Saudi Arabia, the dominant power in the political, economic and military group, is trying to find a compromise to ensure full attendance at the summit.
Bahrain has said it would boycott the summit in protest against Qatar's failure to withdraw a case it has taken to the International Court of Justice over their territorial dispute.
Qatar said it would only withdraw the case if Saudi mediation succeeded in settling the long-standing row over a cluster of islands potentially rich in natural gas.
